==Problem==

Niki usually leaves her cell phone on. If her cell phone is on but
she is not actually using it, the battery will last for <math>24</math> hours. If
she is using it constantly, the battery will last for only <math>3</math> hours.
Since the last recharge, her phone has been on <math>9</math> hours, and during
that time she has used it for <math>60</math> minutes. If she doesn’t use it any
more but leaves the phone on, how many more hours will the battery last?

<math>\textbf{(A)}\ 7 \qquad \textbf{(B)}\ 8 \qquad \textbf{(C)}\ 11 \qquad \textbf{(D)}\ 14 \qquad \textbf{(E)}\ 15</math>

==Solution==
When not being used, the cell phone uses up <math>\frac{1}{24}</math> of its battery per hour. When being used, the cell phone uses up <math>\frac{1}{3}</math> of its battery per hour. Since Niki's phone has been on for <math>9</math> hours, of those <math>8</math> simply on and <math>1</math> with Niki using her phone, <math>8(\frac{1}{24}) + 1(\frac{1}{3}) = \frac{2}{3}</math> of its battery has been used up. To drain the remaining <math>\frac{1}{3}</math> the phone can last for <math>\frac{\frac{1}{3}}{\frac{1}{24}}=\boxed{\textbf{(B)}\ 8}</math> more hours without being used.
